source.title: Architecture-agnostic Lipschitz-constant Bayesian header and its application to resolve semantically proximal classification errors with vision transformers
source.authors: Frederik Schäfer; L. Mandl; Lars Kälber; T. Ricken

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the effect of random label corruption on clean validation accuracy, but does not measure whether the networks fit corrupted training labels.
record.gate_note: The study reports clean validation accuracy under random label corruption, but no training error on corrupted labels. Its SPCE results concern structured corruption and do not bear on the random-label versions.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4's generalization component in a new setting: pretrained ViT classifiers on four medical and industrial datasets under increasing random label corruption. It does not measure memorization or perfect training fit.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but abbreviated. The authors report roughly 1.46% average accuracy degradation under random corruption versus 6.2% under semantic corruption, and conclude that their Lipschitz-constrained Bayesian head stabilizes uncertainty estimates and improves label-noise identification. They do not establish random-label memorization.
record.recipe_differences: Trains vision-transformer classifiers with random or semantic label corruption and evaluates clean validation accuracy; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Corruption type changes the reported accuracy degradation: random misclassification averages 1.46%, while SPCE averages 6.2%.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 5 shows that a ResNet trained for 40 epochs on semantically corrupted labels incorporates mislabeled patterns into its feature clusters despite optimal clean validation accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic label corruption can alter learned representations even at the checkpoint with highest clean validation accuracy.

record.problems: Random corruption results are reported as an average across models without an uncertainty estimate in the relevant text. Corruption is tested only through 15%, and no training error on corrupted labels is reported.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit real versus random labels and convergence slowdown with increasing corruption. Appendix A's epoch timings do not provide these comparisons.
Training to zero error on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs. Inference-time corruption experiments do not test this.

Perfect training fit while memorizing noise; degradation above 15% corruption toward chance; and a strictly steady decline at individual corruption rates, which the readable aggregate does not establish.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it preserves true-label generalization.
Temporal ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noise. Figure 5 shows a final feature representation under semantic corruption, without a learning trajectory.

record.verdict_notes: The original limits_scope verdict confuses untested components with demonstrated failures. Neither the low corruption ceiling nor absent training-error measurements establishes a limitation of V4.

versions.untested_parts: Whether completely random labels can be fit to zero or near-zero training error, with test error at chance and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training time relative to true-label training and convergence as corruption increases.
Whether training error remains perfect; corruption levels above 15%; whether test error rises steadily toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels over training.

rows.subject: all models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Trained models with randomly misclassified labels at rates from 1% to 15%; measured clean validation accuracy.
rows.note: The paper reports this aggregate degradation; it does not give training error on the corrupted labels.
rows.check: The reported 1.46% average clean-validation accuracy decline supports the measured degradation component. Missing training-error measurements do not make that observed decline partial. The aggregate does not establish a strictly steady decline at every corruption rate. Figure 1's caption says training accuracy, but its axes and §3 identify clean validation accuracy; no perfect training fit can be inferred.

relationships.condition: Generalization component only: random label corruption through 15%, averaged across the compared models and four datasets
relationships.reason: R1 reports a 1.46% average decline in clean validation accuracy as random corruption increases, consistent with degradation over this low-noise range; it does not establish simultaneous perfect training fit.
relationships.display_finding: Clean validation accuracy declined by an average of 1.46% across the compared models and four datasets.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Random label corruption through η = 15%, aggregated across models
reader_labels.reason: Clean validation accuracy degrades by an average of 1.46%, but the study does not establish perfect training fit or test behavior through complete corruption (R1).
